name: Helix Biosystems Sanguine Carrier Implant
description:
The Sanguine Carrier Implant is a subcutaneous communication device that uses the body's own cardiovascular system as a transmission medium, encoding low-bandwidth data signals onto the electrical noise of the user's heartbeat and transmitting them via conductive dermal patches to a paired receiver unit in skin-to-skin contact. Helix Biosystems originally developed the technology for their medical monitoring division — the implant's architecture derives from cardiac telemetry systems used to track patients in environments where wireless transmission was prohibited. The communication application emerged from the same research, when engineers realized the body-conducted signal was effectively invisible to any external monitoring system that wasn't physically touching the user.

The implant itself is a rice-grain-sized node placed in the forearm's subcutaneous layer during a minor outpatient procedure. It draws power from the body's ambient bioelectric field and requires no external battery. Data is encoded onto cardiac electrical patterns at a rate low enough to be indistinguishable from normal physiological noise, then transmitted through conductive contact — a handshake, a touch on the shoulder, skin contact through thin fabric. The paired receiver decodes the signal and renders it as text or audio through a connected earpiece or display. The effective bandwidth supports text messaging and simple numeric codes; voice is possible but heavily compressed.

The Sanguine Implant's most significant attribute is its absolute invisibility to conventional surveillance. There is no wireless transmission to intercept, no device to confiscate, and no signal to jam. Communication requires only physical proximity and contact — a limitation that has shaped an entire subculture of tactile signaling protocols among its users. Helix markets it for medical and accessibility applications, and the dual-use communication function exists in a legal gray zone that the company has never moved to clarify.

cultural_context: In GLMZ, the Sanguine Implant occupies a unique social position — because it is technically a medical device, even individuals in heavily surveilled corporate housing can carry one without legal exposure. This has made it extraordinarily popular among labor organizers, political dissidents, and anyone who needs to communicate in spaces where every other option is compromised. There is an entire subculture of tactile code languages developed by Sanguine users, some of which have become recognizable to corporate security — which has in turn driven further elaboration of the codes.
known_users: Political dissidents operating inside corporate facilities
Accessibility advocates who discovered the communication function
story_hooks: A Sanguine user is found dead in a corporate facility with no apparent cause — but their implant has been transmitting continuously for 11 hours since death, and someone is still receiving.

An elaborate tactile code language used by a dissident network has been partially decoded by corporate security. The players need to warn the network before the next meeting — but they can only reach members through touch.

Helix Biosystems quietly issues a firmware update to all Sanguine implants. Users with older nodes start reporting that their transmissions are being echoed — something is receiving their signals that isn't their paired unit.

A corporate executive's Sanguine implant has been secretly paired to an unauthorized receiver by someone who had physical contact with them for long enough to negotiate the handshake. Someone has been reading everything they've transmitted for months.
